sub: Web architecture, client-server communication, HTTP/HTTPS, DNS and hosting
def: Web architecture is the stateless client-server model in which a client requests a URL-named resource over HTTP or its TLS-protected form HTTPS, DNS translates the hostname into an address to reach, and hosting infrastructure serves the response, often with caches and proxies interposed between the two ends.
exp:
The web began as a request-response system for static hypertext and every later layer is an accretion on that one idea. A resource is named by a URL, a client asks for it, a server answers, and the protocol keeps no memory of the exchange. Statelessness is the design decision everything else pays for: because no server holds conversational state, any of a hundred identical servers behind a load balancer can answer the next request, which is what makes horizontal scaling cheap. The costs are that identity must be re-established on every request, which is what cookies and bearer tokens exist to do, and that anything expensive must be re-derived or cached. The progression is worth being able to narrate: static files, then CGI spawning a process per request, then persistent application servers rendering HTML per request, then single-page applications that fetch JSON from an API and render on the client, and now edge and serverless execution that pushes the compute back towards the user. Each step moved rendering work across the client-server boundary; none of them changed the request-response core.

HTTP method semantics are examined through two properties that are routinely conflated. A method is safe if it is not intended to change server state, and idempotent if issuing it many times leaves the same state as issuing it once. GET, HEAD and OPTIONS are safe, and everything safe is idempotent. PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe: PUT writes the full representation to a known URL, so a retried PUT overwrites with the same bytes, and a retried DELETE finds the resource already gone. POST is neither, because it asks the server to create a subordinate resource at a URL the server chooses, so a retry creates a second one. PATCH is not idempotent in general, because a patch document like increment balance by 100 applies twice. This is exactly why a client that times out and retries can safely retry a PUT but must not blindly retry a POST, and why creation endpoints that need retry safety carry an idempotency key.

Status codes are the other half of that examination. 200 returns a body; 201 Created should carry a Location header naming the new resource; 204 No Content deliberately has no body. In the redirect family 301 and 308 are permanent and 302 and 307 temporary, and the distinction that matters is method preservation: 301 and 302 have historically been rewritten by clients into a GET, while 307 and 308 preserve the original method and body. 304 Not Modified is a cache validation answer and carries no body, which is the whole point of it. Conditional requests drive that: the server sends an ETag, the client sends it back as If-None-Match, and an unchanged resource costs a header exchange instead of a payload; the Last-Modified and If-Modified-Since pair does the same on a timestamp. Turned round for writes, If-Match gives optimistic concurrency, and a mismatch is 412 Precondition Failed. In the error ranges, 400 is a malformed request, 401 means not authenticated and should carry WWW-Authenticate, 403 means authenticated but not permitted, 405 means the URL exists but not for that method, 409 is a conflict, 429 is rate limiting, 500 is an unhandled server fault, 502 a bad upstream answer and 504 an upstream timeout, which is why a reverse proxy in front of a dead PHP-FPM pool returns 502 rather than 500.

Caching is controlled by Cache-Control, and its two most-confused values are no-cache, which permits storage but requires revalidation before reuse, and no-store, which forbids writing the response down at all. max-age sets freshness in seconds, private restricts storage to the end client rather than a shared proxy or CDN, and stale-while-revalidate lets a stale copy be served while a fresh one is fetched behind it. Transport has evolved underneath all of this without changing the semantics: HTTP/1.1 added persistent connections but still serialises responses on a connection, so browsers opened several connections per host; HTTP/2 multiplexes many streams over one TCP connection with header compression, removing protocol-level head-of-line blocking but not TCP's, since one lost segment stalls every stream; HTTP/3 moves to QUIC over UDP with per-stream loss recovery, which removes that too.

HTTPS is HTTP carried inside TLS. The handshake negotiates a cipher suite, the server presents a certificate chain that the client validates to a trusted root, and an ephemeral key agreement produces session keys that give forward secrecy. Two extensions in the ClientHello matter for hosting. Server Name Indication carries the hostname the client wants before the certificate is chosen, which is the only reason hundreds of HTTPS sites can share one IP address; the HTTP Host header cannot serve that role because it is inside the encrypted stream and is not read until after the certificate has already been sent. ALPN negotiates which application protocol, HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2, will run inside the tunnel. HSTS is a response header that tells the browser to use HTTPS for this host for a stated period, which closes the plaintext first hop before a redirect; it encrypts nothing itself and does nothing to a browser that has never visited the site unless the domain is on the preload list.

DNS resolution walks a delegation. A stub resolver asks a recursive resolver, which asks a root server for the TLD's nameservers, the TLD server for the zone's authoritative nameservers, and the authoritative server for the record, caching each answer for its TTL. Record types are directly examinable: A maps a name to an IPv4 address, AAAA to IPv6, CNAME aliases one name to another and cannot legally sit alongside other records at the zone apex, which is why providers offer ALIAS or ANAME pseudo-records for a bare domain pointed at a CDN. MX names mail exchangers with a preference value where lower wins, TXT carries SPF, DKIM and ownership verification strings, NS delegates a zone, SOA holds the zone's serial and timing parameters, PTR does reverse lookup, SRV names a service with host and port, and CAA restricts which certificate authorities may issue for the domain. Propagation delay is a misnomer: nothing is pushed anywhere, and the delay is simply resolvers holding cached answers for the old TTL. That is why the discipline before a migration is to lower the TTL, for example from 86400 to 300, at least one old-TTL period in advance, cut over, then raise it again.

Hosting shades from shared hosting through VPS and dedicated servers to cloud instances, containers and serverless functions, with a CDN in front caching static assets at edge points of presence and forwarding misses to the origin. Name-based virtual hosting is the mechanism common to all of them: one IP address, many sites, disambiguated by Host for cleartext HTTP and by SNI for TLS.

Exam shape: the MCQ half draws almost mechanically from this leaf, with status-code attribution, method idempotency, DNS record purpose and the SNI-versus-Host distinction being the standing favourites. It is also essay-shaped in the conventional half, where explain the working of DNS with the steps of an iterative and a recursive query, or describe the client-server model of the web and the role of HTTP and HTTPS, are questions the paper can set every year. Marks are lost by writing the narrative without naming the mechanisms, so anchor each paragraph to a concrete artefact, a header, a record type or a status code.
facts: Safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS) do not intend to change state and are all idempotent; PUT and DELETE are idempotent but not safe; POST and PATCH are neither.
304 Not Modified is returned to a conditional request whose validator still matches, and it carries no message body; If-Match failing on a write yields 412 Precondition Failed.
401 Unauthorized means authentication is missing or invalid and should accompany a WWW-Authenticate header; 403 Forbidden means the identity is known but not permitted.
307 and 308 preserve the original method and body across a redirect, whereas 301 and 302 have historically been rewritten by clients into a GET.
Cache-Control: no-cache allows the response to be stored but requires revalidation before reuse; no-store forbids storing it at all.
Server Name Indication travels in the TLS ClientHello and is what lets one IP address serve many HTTPS sites; the HTTP Host header arrives too late, inside the encrypted stream.
HTTP/2 multiplexes streams over a single TCP connection and so removes HTTP-level head-of-line blocking, but not TCP-level blocking; HTTP/3 over QUIC removes that as well.
A CNAME cannot coexist with other record types at the zone apex, which is why providers supply ALIAS or ANAME records for a bare domain.
MX records carry a preference number in which the lowest value is the most preferred mail exchanger.
Lowering a record's TTL before a migration works because resolvers expire cached answers sooner; no push mechanism exists and the registrar and root servers are not involved in the change.
traps: Host header versus SNI: both name the site, but only SNI is available when the server must choose a TLS certificate, because the Host header is not readable until the encrypted tunnel already exists.

Idempotent is not the same as safe. A stem asking which method may be retried after a timeout without duplicating a resource wants PUT, not GET (which would not have created anything) and not POST (which duplicates).
DNS propagation is caching expiry, not distribution. An option claiming the registrar pushes the change to root servers, or that the old server starts refusing connections, is wrong on mechanism.
HSTS is not encryption and not a replacement for a valid certificate; it only instructs a browser that has already visited the site to refuse plaintext for that host.
mnem: Safe is a subset of idempotent: safe methods only read, idempotent methods may write but land in the same place however many times you send them. POST is outside both circles.

sub: HTML, semantic elements, forms, multimedia, Canvas, SVG and accessibility
def: This leaf covers HTML as document structure rather than presentation: elements that carry meaning and landmark roles, the submission and validation behaviour of form controls, embedded audio, video and responsive images, the two graphics models offered by canvas and SVG, and the WCAG-based accessibility standards a public web application must meet.
exp:
Semantic markup is not decoration; it is the only structural information assistive technology, search crawlers and reader modes have. Elements such as header, nav, main, article, section, aside, footer, figure with figcaption, and time carry an implicit ARIA landmark or role, so a screen-reader user can jump between regions the way a sighted user scans a page. There should be exactly one main per document, and header and footer map to the banner and contentinfo landmarks only when they are page-level rather than nested inside an article or section. The section-versus-div line is the one MPSC likes: section is a thematic grouping that should have a heading, while div carries no meaning at all and exists purely to hang styling or scripting on. Headings are the other navigation surface, and the rule is that h1 to h6 express document outline, not font size; skipping from h2 to h4 because the smaller size looked better breaks the outline for anyone navigating by headings, and CSS is the correct tool for the size.

Forms are the highest-density source of small factual questions in this leaf. A control is submitted only if it has a name attribute, is inside the form, and is not disabled; readonly controls are submitted, disabled ones are not, which is the pair examiners set against each other. A checkbox is submitted only when checked and its value defaults to the string on if none is given. A button element inside a form with no type attribute defaults to type submit, so clicking it submits the form even though the developer intended a plain click handler; type must be written out explicitly to get the inert behaviour. Labels are associated either by wrapping the control or by a for attribute matching the control's id, and a placeholder is not a substitute, because it disappears on first keystroke, is not a dependable accessible name, and usually fails contrast requirements. fieldset with legend groups related controls, which is how a set of radio buttons gets a group-level question announced. Input types email, url, tel, number, date, range and file, together with required, pattern, min, max, step and maxlength, drive the browser's constraint validation, exposed to script as checkValidity, reportValidity and setCustomValidity and to CSS as the validity pseudo-classes. The submission encoding defaults to application/x-www-form-urlencoded and must be changed to multipart/form-data for a file upload; a GET form puts its fields in the query string, a POST form in the request body. None of this is security. Client-side validation is a user-experience feature and every constraint must be re-checked on the server, because the request can be replayed with any body an attacker likes.

For multimedia, the audio and video elements take controls, poster, preload and muted attributes, hold one or more source children so the browser can pick a format it supports, and take track children pointing at WebVTT files for captions, subtitles and descriptions. Unmuted autoplay is blocked by browsers by policy, so an autoplaying video must be muted. Responsive images use srcset with sizes to let the browser pick a resolution, and picture with source and media to art-direct a different crop at a different breakpoint. The alt attribute has three states and only two are ever correct: descriptive alt text for a meaningful image, alt with an empty string for a purely decorative one so assistive technology skips it, and a missing alt attribute, which is the defect, because the technology then falls back to announcing the file name.

Canvas and SVG solve the same problem from opposite ends and the choice is a standing exam item. Canvas is immediate mode: you obtain a 2D context and issue drawing calls that write pixels into a bitmap, and the moment a call returns the browser retains no knowledge of what was drawn. There is no node per shape, so there is no layout, no hit testing and no per-object memory, which is why a scatter plot of fifty thousand points redrawn on every drag belongs on a canvas. The costs follow from the same fact: nothing is individually selectable or styleable, redrawing means redrawing everything, the output is resolution-dependent, and it is invisible to assistive technology unless you supply fallback content inside the element and mirror the state some accessible way. A canvas has two independent sizes, the width and height content attributes that set the backing bitmap and the CSS width and height that scale it; setting only the CSS size stretches a small bitmap and produces the familiar blurred canvas, and on a high-density display the bitmap must be sized by the device pixel ratio and the context scaled to match. SVG is retained mode: every circle, path and text run is a real DOM node, so it can be styled with CSS, animated, given its own event listener, and made accessible with a title, a desc and an appropriate role. It scales without loss because the viewBox defines a user coordinate system that is mapped onto whatever size the element is given. Its weakness is exactly its strength, since tens of thousands of nodes cost tens of thousands of nodes' worth of layout and hit testing.

Accessibility standards resolve to WCAG, whose four principles are that content must be perceivable, operable, understandable and robust, with conformance stated at level A, AA or AAA; AA is the level public procurement normally requires, and it is where the familiar contrast ratios of 4.5 to 1 for body text and 3 to 1 for large text sit. Indian government portals are additionally written against the Guidelines for Indian Government Websites, which are built on WCAG and are the reason accessibility appears on a state services examination at all. The practical rules are short. Everything reachable by mouse must be reachable and operable by keyboard, in a sensible focus order, with a visible focus indicator. tabindex of 0 puts an element in the natural tab order and minus 1 makes it focusable only by script; positive values reorder the whole document and should not be used. The first rule of ARIA is not to use ARIA when a native element already carries the semantics, because a button element is focusable, keyboard-activatable and announced correctly for free while a div with role button gives you only the announcement and leaves you to reimplement the rest. Where ARIA is needed, aria-label and aria-labelledby supply an accessible name, aria-describedby attaches supplementary text such as an error message, and a live region announces content that changes without a page load.

Exam shape: the MCQ half is dense here and mostly factual, on default form behaviour, which element carries which landmark, the canvas-versus-SVG trade-off, and what makes a control inaccessible. The conventional half sets this leaf as an essay on accessibility, typically describe the accessibility requirements of a government web portal and how they are achieved, where the marks come from naming principles and concrete techniques together rather than writing about inclusion in the abstract.
facts: A form control is submitted only if it has a name attribute and is not disabled; readonly controls are submitted, disabled controls are not.
A button element inside a form with no type attribute defaults to type submit, so clicking it submits the form.
A checkbox is submitted only when checked, and its value defaults to the string on if no value attribute is given.
A file upload requires the form's enctype to be multipart/form-data; the default is application/x-www-form-urlencoded.
alt with an empty string marks an image as decorative so assistive technology skips it; omitting alt entirely is a defect, because the file name is announced instead.

Canvas is immediate-mode and keeps no node per drawn object, so it has no per-shape hit testing, no per-shape styling and no built-in accessibility; SVG is retained-mode and every shape is a scriptable, styleable, individually accessible DOM node.
A canvas element's width and height attributes set the backing bitmap size, while CSS width and height only scale it; setting only the CSS size produces a stretched, blurred drawing.

WCAG is organised around four principles, perceivable, operable, understandable and robust, with conformance levels A, AA and AAA; AA requires a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1 for normal-size text.
tabindex of 0 places an element in the natural tab order and minus 1 makes it focusable by script only; positive tabindex values reorder the entire document and are discouraged.
There should be exactly one main element per document, and header and footer map to the banner and contentinfo landmarks only at page level, not when nested inside an article or section.
traps: A placeholder is not a label. It vanishes on first keystroke, is not a reliable accessible name, and the fix is a label element associated by for and id, not more placeholder text.

Client-side constraint validation attributes such as required and pattern are a usability feature, never a security control; the same request can be sent without a browser, so the server must revalidate.

Canvas versus SVG is decided by object count and interaction, not by capability. Both can be scripted and both support gradients and transparency; canvas wins on tens of thousands of objects redrawn continuously, SVG wins when each object must be selectable, styleable or accessible.
disabled versus readonly: both stop the user editing, but only readonly still sends the field's value with the form, so disabling a field silently drops it from the submitted data.
mnem: WCAG is POUR: Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust. For graphics, Canvas paints and forgets, SVG draws and remembers.

sub: CSS, Flexbox, Grid and responsive web design
def: CSS is the declarative language that maps document structure onto visual presentation through a cascade resolved by origin, specificity and source order, with Flexbox distributing items along a single axis, Grid laying out rows and columns together, and responsive design adapting both to viewport and container size.
exp:
Everything in CSS starts with how a declaration wins. The cascade resolves conflicts by origin and importance first, then by specificity, then by source order, and only the last of those is about which rule you wrote later. Specificity is counted as three numbers, the count of id selectors, then the count of class, attribute and pseudo-class selectors, then the count of element and pseudo-element selectors, and the comparison is lexicographic. So the selector nav ul li a scores 0-0-4 and the selector .menu a scores 0-1-1, and the second wins outright, because one class beats any number of element selectors no matter how long the chain. Add an id and #nav a at 1-0-1 beats both. Inline style attributes outrank all selectors, and a declaration marked important outranks normal declarations in the same origin, which is why an important rule in a stylesheet defeats an inline style that is not itself important. The universal selector and combinators contribute nothing, and :not and :is contribute the specificity of their most specific argument rather than of themselves. Inheritance is a separate mechanism from the cascade: text-level properties such as color, font-family and line-height inherit to descendants, while box-level properties such as margin, padding, border and background do not, and the keywords inherit, initial, unset and revert let you override either way explicitly.

The box model is the other foundation. By default width sizes only the content box, so padding and border are added outside it and a declared width of 200px with 20px of padding and a 1px border occupies 242px; box-sizing set to border-box makes the declared width include padding and border, which is why almost every real stylesheet sets it globally. Adjacent vertical margins collapse to the larger of the two, and a parent's top margin collapses with its first child's unless a border, padding, or a new formatting context intervenes; horizontal margins never collapse, and margins do not collapse between flex or grid items at all. Positioning follows: static and relative stay in flow, absolute is positioned against the nearest ancestor that is itself positioned, fixed is positioned against the viewport, and sticky behaves as relative until a scroll threshold and then as fixed within its scroll container. The exception worth carrying is that a transform, filter or will-change on an ancestor establishes a containing block, so a fixed child inside a transformed parent stops tracking the viewport. z-index applies only to positioned elements and to flex and grid children, and it is resolved within a stacking context, which opacity below 1, transforms, filters and isolation all create, so a high z-index inside a low-stacked context cannot climb out of it.

Flexbox is one-dimensional: it lays out along one axis and handles the other as an afterthought. flex-direction sets the main axis and the cross axis is perpendicular to it, so all the alignment vocabulary swaps meaning when direction becomes column. justify-content distributes items along the main axis, align-items aligns them on the cross axis within their line, align-self overrides that for one item, and align-content distributes multiple lines on the cross axis and therefore does nothing at all unless flex-wrap is set to wrap, since a nowrap container has exactly one line. The flex shorthand is grow, shrink, basis, defaulting to 0 1 auto, and the common shorthand flex 1 expands to 1 1 0. Distribution is arithmetic worth doing by hand. Three items with basis 100px each in a 500px container leave 200px of free space; with grow factors 1, 1 and 3 the free space is divided into five shares of 40px, giving final widths of 140, 140 and 220. Shrinking is weighted differently: it scales the shrink factor by the base size, so two items with bases of 200px and shrink factors 1 and 3 in a 300px container have a 100px overflow to absorb against weighted bases of 200 and 600, and they end up at 175px and 125px rather than at 75 and 25.

Grid is two-dimensional, and it uses inline and block axis terminology rather than flexbox's main and cross. grid-template-columns and grid-template-rows define explicit tracks; the fr unit is a share of the leftover space after fixed sizes and gaps are taken; repeat, minmax, min-content, max-content and fit-content size tracks declaratively; gap replaces margin hacks for gutters. Anything placed outside the explicit tracks lands in the implicit grid, sized by grid-auto-rows and grid-auto-columns and placed according to grid-auto-flow. Items can be positioned by line number, by named lines, or by drawing the layout with grid-template-areas, which is the clearest form for a page shell. On the container, justify-content and align-content distribute the tracks inside a larger container while justify-items and align-items position each item inside its own cell, and that pairing is a routine exam distinction. The responsive idiom to know is grid-template-columns set to repeat with auto-fill and minmax of 220px and 1fr: it fits as many 220px-minimum columns as the width allows, drops to fewer as the container narrows, and shares any leftover space equally through the 1fr maximum. auto-fill and auto-fit differ only when there are more tracks than items, where auto-fill keeps the empty tracks and auto-fit collapses them, which with a 1fr maximum lets the remaining items stretch to fill the row.

Responsive design is then a policy layered on those tools. The precondition is the viewport meta tag declaring width equal to device-width with an initial scale of 1; without it a mobile browser assumes a desktop-width virtual viewport and renders the whole desktop layout scaled down, so perfectly correct media queries never match and the page merely looks shrunk. Beyond that, work mobile-first with min-width media queries so the base stylesheet is the small-screen case and each query adds rather than undoes; choose breakpoints where the content stops working rather than at named device sizes; size type and spacing in rem and em, use percentages, viewport units and clamp for fluid ranges, and prefer intrinsic sizing so the layout adapts without a query at all. Container queries let a component respond to the width of its own container rather than the viewport, which is what a reusable component actually needs. Media features beyond width matter too, particularly prefers-reduced-motion and prefers-color-scheme, and images should be served responsively with srcset and sizes rather than by shipping one large file.

Exam shape: MCQ items on this leaf are usually one-step reasoning, give a declaration and ask what layout results, or give two selectors and ask which wins. The conventional half sets it as design a responsive layout for a given page and explain your use of Flexbox and Grid, where marks come from justifying the one-dimensional versus two-dimensional choice and from remembering the viewport meta tag and relative units, not from reciting property names.
facts: Specificity is compared as ids first, then classes, attributes and pseudo-classes, then elements and pseudo-elements; a single class selector beats a chain of any number of element selectors.
align-content in Flexbox distributes multiple lines on the cross axis and has no effect unless flex-wrap is set to wrap, because a nowrap container has only one line.
The flex shorthand is grow, shrink and basis with a default of 0 1 auto, and flex: 1 expands to 1 1 0.
Flex growth divides free space in proportion to the grow factors alone, whereas flex shrinkage weights each shrink factor by the item's flex base size.

In Grid, repeat(auto-fill, minmax(220px, 1fr)) fits as many columns of at least 220px as the width allows and shares leftover space equally; auto-fit differs only by collapsing empty tracks when items run out.
box-sizing: border-box makes a declared width include padding and border; the default content-box adds them outside the declared width.
z-index applies only to positioned elements and flex or grid children, and it is resolved within the nearest stacking context, which opacity below 1, transform, filter and isolation each create.
A transform, filter or will-change on an ancestor establishes a containing block, so a descendant with position: fixed is positioned against that ancestor instead of the viewport.

Without a viewport meta tag declaring width=device-width and initial-scale=1, a mobile browser lays the page out in a desktop-width virtual viewport and scales the result down, so width-based media queries never match.
Flexbox describes its axes as main and cross, which swap when flex-direction is column; Grid uses inline and block axes instead.
traps: flex: 1 1 0 does not equalise widths regardless of content. Flex items default to min-width: auto, so an item is never narrower than its min-content size and a single unbreakable token defeats the zero basis; true equalisation also needs min-width: 0.

justify-content versus align-content in Flexbox: the first distributes items along the main axis and always applies, the second distributes wrapped lines on the cross axis and does nothing in a single-line container.
auto-fill versus auto-fit: they behave identically while there are enough items to fill the row and differ only in whether leftover empty tracks are kept or collapsed.
Specificity is not selector length. A four-element descendant chain scores 0-0-4 and still loses to one class at 0-1-0, and adding more ancestors to the chain never fixes an overridden rule.
When flex-direction is column, justify-content controls vertical placement and align-items controls horizontal placement; candidates apply the row-direction meanings and pick the wrong property.
mnem: Justify runs along the main axis, align crosses it. In Grid, auto-fill keeps the empty tracks, auto-fit collapses them.

sub: JavaScript, the DOM, event handling, asynchronous programming, JSON and Fetch
def: JavaScript is the single-threaded, event-driven language of the browser; the DOM is the mutable object model of the parsed document it manipulates; events propagate through capture, target and bubble phases; and asynchrony is expressed through promises resolved by an event loop that drains microtasks between tasks, with JSON as the wire format and Fetch as the HTTP client.
exp:
Start with the language properties that produce exam questions. Declarations with var are hoisted and initialised to undefined, while let and const are hoisted but sit in a temporal dead zone until the declaration is evaluated, so reading them early throws rather than yielding undefined; const binds the reference, not the contents, so a const array can still be pushed to. Functions are first-class and close over the variable bindings of their defining scope, which is what makes a factory function or a private counter work, and the classic loop bug where var shares one binding across all iterations while let creates a fresh binding per iteration. The value of this is determined by call site, not by definition site, for ordinary functions, with the four cases being a bare call, a method call, an explicit call with call, apply or bind, and construction with new; arrow functions have no this of their own and take it lexically, which is why an arrow is the right callback inside a method and the wrong choice for an object literal method. Comparison should be made with the strict operators, because the loose ones apply a coercion table nobody remembers correctly.

The DOM is the object model over the parsed document, and the working knowledge is which access returns what. querySelector and querySelectorAll take CSS selectors, and the NodeList returned by querySelectorAll is static, a snapshot at call time, whereas getElementsByTagName and getElementsByClassName return live HTMLCollections that keep changing under you, which is how a loop that removes elements while iterating goes wrong. Writing to textContent inserts a text node and never parses markup; writing to innerHTML parses the string as HTML, which is a script-injection sink; innerText additionally respects styling and therefore forces layout to be recalculated. Mutating the tree is expensive because it invalidates layout, so batch by building a DocumentFragment offline and appending once, and avoid layout thrashing, which is the pattern of reading a geometry property such as offsetHeight and then writing a style in the same loop, forcing a synchronous reflow on every iteration; read everything first, then write.

Event handling has three phases: an event descends from the root to the target in the capture phase, fires at the target, and then bubbles back up, and addEventListener attaches to the bubble phase unless capture is requested. Inside a handler, currentTarget is the element the listener is attached to and target is the deepest element the event originated on, which is the whole basis of event delegation: attach one listener to a stable ancestor such as a table body, read event.target inside it, and rows created after page load are handled without ever attaching a listener to them. stopPropagation halts further travel along the tree, stopImmediatePropagation additionally prevents other listeners on the same element from running, and preventDefault cancels the browser's default action such as form submission or link navigation while leaving propagation intact, so they are not substitutes for one another. Some events do not bubble, notably focus and blur, whose bubbling counterparts are focusin and focusout. Listener options include once, signal for removal through an AbortController, and passive, which promises not to call preventDefault so the browser need not block scrolling on the handler.

Asynchronous execution rests on one runtime thread and an event loop with two queues of unequal standing. A task, sometimes called a macrotask, is a unit such as a timer callback, an I/O completion or a dispatched event. Microtasks are promise reaction jobs and anything scheduled with queueMicrotask. The rule is that after the currently running task's stack empties, the entire microtask queue is drained, including microtasks that other microtasks enqueue, before the loop takes the next task or renders a frame. So in the script that logs A, schedules a zero-delay timeout logging B, resolves a promise whose then logs C, runs an async function that logs D, awaits, then logs E, and finally logs F, the output is A, D, F, then C, E, then B. The synchronous body runs first in source order, the promise continuation and the resumption after await are microtasks and both run before the timer, and setTimeout with zero delay only means as soon as possible at the start of a future task, never immediately. This is also why an infinite chain of microtasks starves rendering while a chain of timers does not. Promise combinators are examinable in their own right: all rejects as soon as any input rejects, allSettled always fulfils with a per-promise status record, race settles with the first settlement of either kind, and any fulfils with the first fulfilment and rejects only if every input rejects.

JSON is a data interchange format that resembles JavaScript object literal syntax without being a subset of it in either direction. Keys must be double-quoted strings, single quotes, comments, trailing commas, undefined and function values have no representation, and NaN and Infinity are not expressible. That drives what JSON.stringify does: object properties whose values are undefined, functions or symbols are omitted from the output entirely, the same values inside an array become null because array position must be preserved, NaN and Infinity serialise as null, a Date is serialised through its toJSON method into an ISO 8601 string, and a circular reference throws. JSON.parse performs no reviving of its own, so a serialised date comes back as a string and must be reconstructed, which is what the reviver argument is for.

Fetch returns a promise that resolves as soon as the response headers arrive, for any status the server sends. A 500 with a JSON error body resolves with a Response whose ok is false and whose status is 500; the promise rejects only for a network-level failure, a CORS block or an abort. Forgetting to test response.ok before calling response.json is the most common error on this leaf, because the body then parses as an error document and flows into the success path. The body is a stream and can be consumed only once, so calling both text and json on the same response fails. Requests are cancelled by passing an AbortController's signal, which is also how a superseded request is dropped. Credentials are governed by the credentials option, whose same-origin default means cookies are not attached to cross-origin requests unless include is specified, and the server must then answer with Access-Control-Allow-Credentials and a specific origin rather than a wildcard. Cross-origin requests are governed by the same-origin policy: a simple request goes straight out and only the reading of the response is gated, while a request using a method beyond GET, HEAD or POST, or a Content-Type other than the three form encodings, or custom headers such as Authorization, is preceded by an OPTIONS preflight that the server must answer with the allowed origin, methods and headers. Sending JSON therefore preflights, and sending a urlencoded form does not. CORS is a browser-enforced relaxation of the same-origin policy, not a server-side access control, and it protects the user's other sites rather than your API.

One loading detail belongs here because it is asked directly. For an external classic script, async downloads in parallel and executes the moment it is ready, in no guaranteed order and possibly interrupting parsing; defer downloads in parallel and executes after parsing completes, in document order, just before DOMContentLoaded. Module scripts behave as deferred by default.

Exam shape: this leaf supplies most of the code-output questions in the unit, so expect a six-line fragment with a timer and a promise and be able to reason the queue order rather than remember an answer. The conventional half asks it as explain the JavaScript event loop with microtasks and macrotasks, or write a client that fetches and renders JSON with error handling, where the marks are in checking response.ok and handling rejection separately from an error status.
facts: The entire microtask queue is drained after the current task and before the next task or a render, so a resolved promise's callback always runs before a setTimeout scheduled with zero delay in the same script.
event.currentTarget is the element the listener is attached to; event.target is the deepest element the event originated on, and delegation depends on that difference.
preventDefault cancels the default action but not propagation; stopPropagation stops travel up or down the tree; stopImmediatePropagation also blocks other listeners on the same element.
querySelectorAll returns a static NodeList snapshot, while getElementsByTagName and getElementsByClassName return live HTMLCollections that update as the document changes.
A fetch promise rejects only on network failure, a CORS block or an abort; any completed HTTP response including 404 and 500 resolves, so response.ok must be tested explicitly.
A Response body is a single-use stream, so json() and text() cannot both be called on the same response.
JSON.stringify omits object properties whose values are undefined, functions or symbols, but writes null in their place inside an array, and serialises NaN and Infinity as null.

A cross-origin request is preflighted with OPTIONS when it uses a method beyond GET, HEAD or POST, custom headers, or a Content-Type other than application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data or text/plain; sending application/json therefore preflights.

defer executes external scripts after parsing, in document order, just before DOMContentLoaded, whereas async executes each as soon as it downloads, in no guaranteed order; module scripts are deferred by default.

Promise.all rejects on the first rejection, allSettled always fulfils with per-promise status records, race settles on the first settlement of either kind, and any rejects only if every input rejects.
The credentials option defaults to same-origin, so cookies are not sent cross-origin unless include is set, and the server must then reply with a specific allowed origin rather than a wildcard.
traps: A 500 response is not a fetch rejection. Code written as fetch(...).then(r => r.json()).catch(...) sends a server error straight down the success path, because the catch never fires.
setTimeout with a zero delay does not run immediately or before promise callbacks; it schedules a new task, and every pending microtask runs first.
target versus currentTarget in a delegated handler: currentTarget is always the container the listener sits on, so using it to identify the clicked row returns the container every time.

CORS is enforced by the browser to protect the user, not by the server to protect the API. Relaxing Access-Control-Allow-Origin does not weaken server-side authorisation, and tightening it does not substitute for authorisation checks.
async and defer both download in parallel and are easily swapped in an answer: only defer guarantees execution order and completion of parsing before it runs.
mnem: Microtasks are the queue that jumps the queue: after every task the loop empties them completely, so promises always beat timers.

sub: Frontend frameworks: components, routing, state management and API integration
def: A modern JavaScript frontend framework renders the interface as a declarative function of state, composed from reusable components that receive props and raise events, with a client-side router mapping URLs to component trees, a state layer distinguishing local UI state from cached server data, and asynchronous API calls integrated through effects with explicit loading, error and cancellation handling.
exp:
The central idea a framework buys you is that the view is a pure function of state. Instead of writing imperative DOM mutations that must each be undone correctly, you describe what the interface should look like for the current state and let the framework compute the difference against what is on screen. Some frameworks do that at run time by diffing a virtual representation of the tree and applying the minimal set of real DOM operations; others compile the template ahead of time into fine-grained update instructions bound to individual reactive values, which avoids the diff entirely. The distinction matters for performance discussion but not for the mental model, which is the same in both: render is derived, never hand-edited.

A component is the unit of that derivation. It receives props from its parent, holds its own local state, and communicates upward by invoking callbacks the parent passed down, which is what unidirectional data flow means in practice: props down, events up. Shared state is lifted to the closest common ancestor rather than pushed sideways between siblings. Composition is the reuse mechanism, not inheritance, so a component that needs extra behaviour is wrapped or given children rather than subclassed. Rendering a list requires a key that is a stable identity for the item, typically its primary key from the server, because the reconciler uses keys to decide which existing node corresponds to which new item; using the array index as the key tells the framework that the item at position 2 is always the same item, so inserting at the front or reordering makes it reuse the wrong nodes and carry over the wrong internal state, which shows up as a checkbox that stays ticked next to a different row. The lifecycle is mount, update and unmount, and side effects belong in an effect that runs after the DOM has been committed, with a cleanup function that runs on unmount and again before each re-run, so that subscriptions, timers and listeners are torn down exactly as often as they were created.

Forms come in two shapes and the distinction is asked directly. A controlled input takes its displayed value from component state on every render and installs a change handler that writes each keystroke back into that state, which makes state the single source of truth and lets you validate, format, mask or conditionally disable as the user types. An uncontrolled input lets the DOM node keep its own value and the component reads it through a ref at submission time, which is less code and adequate for a simple form but gives you no hook for live validation. The trap in a controlled input is supplying a value without a change handler, which produces a field the user apparently cannot type in, because every keystroke is immediately overwritten by the unchanged state.

Client-side routing replaces the browser's navigation with a mapping from URL to component tree. The router intercepts link activation, pushes an entry with the History API, matches the new path against a route table and renders the corresponding component without a network round trip for the document, while still supporting the back button and shareable URLs. Routes are usually nested so a layout renders once and only the inner view swaps, take parameters such as /reports/:id, and are lazily loaded so each route's code is a separate bundle chunk fetched on first visit. Guards or loaders run before a protected route renders, redirecting an unauthenticated user to a login route. The classic deployment defect follows from the fact that the server knows nothing about this table: in-app navigation to /reports/7 works because no request is made, but a browser reload asks the server for /reports/7, which has no file, and the server answers 404. The fix is a server-side fallback that serves index.html for any unmatched path so the client router can resolve the URL, written in Nginx as try_files with the request URI falling back to /index.html. Hash-based routing avoids the problem by keeping the path in the fragment, which the server never sees, at the cost of uglier URLs and weaker crawlability.

State management is really two problems that beginners merge. Client state is UI state the browser owns outright, such as which tab is open or what is typed in a filter; server state is a local cache of data that lives somewhere else, and its hard parts are staleness, revalidation, deduplication of in-flight requests and invalidation after a mutation, none of which a plain global store addresses. Escalate deliberately: local state first, lift it when a sibling needs it, use context or an injection mechanism for genuinely cross-cutting values such as the current user, theme or locale, and reach for an external store only when many distant components read and write the same data. Context is a dependency-injection mechanism and not a performance optimisation, since every consumer re-renders when the provided value changes. Whatever the store, updates must be immutable, because change detection compares references: mutating an array in place and then setting the same reference back produces no re-render at all. Derived values should be computed during render or memoised, not stored as a second piece of state, because two sources of truth for the same fact drift apart.

API integration is where the interesting failure modes live. A component that fetches on mount and on every change of a search query must handle three states explicitly, loading, error and data, and must treat an out-of-order response as a correctness problem rather than a performance one. If the user types a query, then a second, the first response can arrive after the second and overwrite the newer results, so the effect's cleanup must abort the superseded request with an AbortController or set a stale flag that makes the late response be ignored. Debouncing reduces how many requests are issued and improves the odds, but it does not guarantee ordering and is not the fix. Beyond that, an optimistic update applies the expected result immediately and rolls it back if the request fails, mutations must invalidate the cached queries they affect, and any API key or secret must live behind a backend, because a build-time environment variable is inlined into the shipped bundle. Rendering strategy is the last axis: client-side rendering ships an empty shell and fetches everything, server-side rendering returns finished HTML and then hydrates it for interactivity, static generation builds pages ahead of time, and the choice is driven by first-paint latency and crawlability rather than by preference.

Exam shape: MCQ items here are scenario questions with one correct diagnosis, on deep-link 404s, controlled inputs, list keys and stale responses. In the conventional half the leaf appears as compare client-side rendering with server-side rendering, or explain component-based architecture and state management in a modern JavaScript framework, and marks are gained by naming the mechanism, unidirectional flow, reconciliation, cache invalidation, rather than by naming products.
facts: Unidirectional data flow means props pass down and events pass up; shared state is lifted to the nearest common ancestor rather than passed between siblings.

List keys must be stable identities such as a server primary key, because the reconciler matches old nodes to new items by key; array indices break on insertion or reordering and carry component state onto the wrong row.

A controlled input renders its value from component state and writes every keystroke back through a change handler; an uncontrolled input keeps its value in the DOM node and is read through a ref at submission.
History-based client routing needs the web server to fall back to index.html for unmatched paths, expressed in Nginx with try_files, or a reloaded deep link returns 404.
An effect's cleanup function runs on unmount and also before each re-run, which is where subscriptions, timers and in-flight requests must be released.
Change detection compares references, so state must be replaced immutably; mutating an object or array in place and setting the same reference back triggers no re-render.
Context or provide-inject is a dependency-injection mechanism whose consumers all re-render when the provided value changes, so it does not by itself reduce rendering work.
Server state needs caching, staleness and invalidation policy, which a plain global client store does not provide; the two kinds of state have different requirements.
Route-level code splitting loads each route's bundle chunk on first visit, which is what keeps initial payload small in a large single-page application.
Build-time environment variables are inlined into the shipped bundle, so no API secret can be kept in frontend configuration.
traps: Out-of-order responses are fixed by cancelling or ignoring the superseded request in the effect's cleanup, not by debouncing. Debouncing lowers request volume but a slow earlier response can still land after a fast later one.
A reloaded deep link returning 404 is a web-server configuration defect, not a router bug; the wrong answers are switching to hash routing or adding a redirect, both of which hide rather than fix it.

Passing value without a change handler to a controlled input produces a field that appears frozen, because state is re-imposed on every render; the reverse error, an uncontrolled field with validation logic, silently validates nothing.
Using the array index as a list key looks correct until items are inserted, removed or reordered, which is exactly when the reconciler needs the key and gets the wrong answer.
mnem: Props down, events up, keys identify. And remember the deep-link rule: the router knows your routes, the server does not, so the server must fall back to the shell.

sub: Backend development in PHP and Python: REST APIs, CRUD, middleware, auth, sessions and ORM
def: Backend development in PHP and Python builds the server side of a web application: resource-oriented REST endpoints implementing CRUD over HTTP methods, a middleware pipeline handling cross-cutting concerns around each handler, authentication and authorisation carried by server-side sessions or signed tokens, and an object-relational mapper translating between domain objects and database rows.
exp:
The two languages the syllabus names have different execution models and the difference explains most of their idioms. PHP is classically share-nothing and request-scoped: a process from a FastCGI process manager pool picks up a request, the script runs from the top, superglobals such as the query and body arrays, the cookie array, the uploaded-file array and the server environment are populated for it, output is written, and the process state is discarded. Nothing survives between requests except what you put in a database, a cache or a session store, which makes the model easy to scale horizontally and awkward for anything long-lived. Python web applications instead run inside a persistent process behind a standard interface, synchronous through WSGI or asynchronous through ASGI, served by an application server such as Gunicorn, uWSGI or Uvicorn sitting behind Nginx as a reverse proxy. Because the interpreter's global lock serialises bytecode execution, CPU-bound work scales by adding worker processes while I O-bound work scales well with asynchronous workers. Django is the batteries-included choice with its own ORM, migrations, admin and template layer; Flask is minimal and assembled from libraries; FastAPI derives request validation and OpenAPI documentation from type annotations and is native to the async model.

REST is an architectural style, not a protocol. Its constraints are a uniform interface over resources identified by URLs, stateless requests that carry everything needed to serve them, cacheable responses, a layered system so a proxy or gateway can sit transparently in the path, and client-server separation. URLs name nouns, ideally plural collections and their members, and the verb lives in the HTTP method rather than in the path, so a POST to /invoices is right and a GET to /getInvoice is not. CRUD maps onto that interface as create with POST to the collection, answered 201 with a Location header naming the new member; read with GET; update with PUT when the client sends a complete replacement representation to a known URL, or PATCH when it sends a partial change; and remove with DELETE, answered 204 when there is nothing to return. Idempotency is the property that decides retry safety after a timeout: PUT and DELETE can be repeated without further effect, so a retried PUT cannot produce a second copy of the resource, while a retried POST creates a second one unless the endpoint honours a client-supplied idempotency key. Beyond the basics, collections need pagination, and cursor pagination is preferred over offset pagination on large or actively written tables because offsets skip or repeat rows when the underlying data shifts; versioning is carried in the path or a header; and validation failures are reported with a structured error body rather than a bare 400.

Middleware is the composition mechanism that keeps cross-cutting concerns out of handlers. A middleware is a callable that receives the request and the next handler in the chain, may inspect or modify the request, may return a response itself and short-circuit the chain, and may post-process the response on the way back out, which is why it is described as an onion around the handler. Typical layers are request logging and correlation ids, CORS headers, compression, rate limiting, session loading, authentication, CSRF token verification and a top-level error handler. Order is a genuine design decision and an examinable one: the error handler must be outermost so it can catch failures in every inner layer, CORS must run before anything that can reject a request or the browser sees a rejection with no CORS headers and reports only an opaque failure, and authentication must precede authorisation because you cannot check a permission before you know who is asking.

Authentication establishes who the caller is, authorisation decides what that identity may do, and conflating them is the standard slip. Sessions are the stateful answer: the server creates a record keyed by a high-entropy identifier, stores it in files, a database or a shared cache such as Redis, and sends only that identifier to the browser in a cookie. In PHP that cookie carries the session id and nothing else; the session array itself never leaves the server, which is why tampering with the cookie can only mean guessing or stealing another id, never editing the contents. That in turn dictates the defences: enough entropy in the identifier, regeneration of the identifier at every privilege change so a fixated session cannot be inherited, an idle timeout and an absolute timeout, and a shared session backend rather than sticky sessions once there is more than one application server. Tokens are the stateless answer: a signed structure such as a JWT whose claims the server verifies on each request without any lookup. The trade is revocation, which now requires a deny list or short expiry with refresh tokens, and the recurring misunderstanding is that a JWT payload is base64url encoded and not encrypted, so it is readable by anyone holding it and must never carry a secret; verification must also pin the expected algorithm rather than trusting the token's own header. Delegated access uses OAuth 2.0, and OpenID Connect layers identity on top of it by adding an ID token, so OAuth alone is authorisation and OIDC is what makes it login. Passwords are stored with a deliberately slow, salted algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2 through the language's own helper functions, never a raw hash like MD5 or SHA-256. Cookie flags carry the rest of the burden: HttpOnly stops JavaScript reading the cookie and therefore limits what an XSS bug can steal, Secure restricts it to HTTPS, and SameSite governs whether the browser attaches it to cross-site requests, which is the flag that bears on CSRF.

An ORM maps table rows onto objects and hides the SQL, with Django's ORM and SQLAlchemy on the Python side and Eloquent and Doctrine on the PHP side. Two patterns are distinguished: Active Record, where the model object carries its own persistence methods, and Data Mapper, where a separate mapper moves data between objects and tables and the model stays persistence-ignorant. The machinery worth naming is the identity map, which guarantees one in-memory object per row per session, the unit of work, which batches changes and flushes them in one transaction, migrations, which version the schema alongside the code, and the loading strategy. Lazy loading fetches a related object only when the attribute is first touched, which is convenient and produces the N+1 problem: a view that fetches 100 orders in one query and then reads the customer name on each issues one query for the list plus one hundred for the relations, 101 in total, and the number scales with the result set rather than with the code. The fix is eager loading, telling the ORM up front to fetch the relations, which Django expresses as a join for forward foreign keys and as a second batched query for reverse and many-to-many relations, and SQLAlchemy as joined or select-in loading. Raising the connection pool size or caching individual rows treats the symptom. Finally, ORMs parameterise generated SQL by default, but that protection ends the moment a raw fragment or string-built filter is introduced, so injection remains possible in ORM code.

Exam shape: MCQ items here are precise and mechanical, on method idempotency, what a session cookie contains, what middleware ordering achieves and how to recognise N+1 from a query count. The conventional half is essay-shaped around design a RESTful API for a given service, listing endpoints, methods, status codes and authentication, or compare session-based and token-based authentication, where the marks are in the trade-offs, revocation, scaling, and storage, rather than in the definitions.
facts: PHP's default session handling sends only the session identifier in the cookie; the session data itself stays server-side in files, a database or a shared cache.
PUT and DELETE are idempotent, so a retried request after a timeout cannot create a second resource; POST is not idempotent and needs a client-supplied idempotency key to be retry-safe.
Creating a resource is answered 201 Created with a Location header; a successful delete with nothing to return is answered 204 No Content.
Middleware wraps the handler as an onion: the error handler belongs outermost, CORS before any layer that can reject a request, and authentication before authorisation.
A JWT payload is base64url encoded and signed, not encrypted, so its claims are readable by anyone holding the token and must contain no secrets; verification must pin the expected algorithm.
OAuth 2.0 provides delegated authorisation; OpenID Connect adds an identity layer with an ID token on top of it, and only that combination constitutes login.
Session identifiers must be regenerated whenever privilege changes, which is what defeats session fixation.
An N+1 query pattern is one query for a list of n rows plus one per row for a lazily loaded relation, n plus 1 in total, and it is removed by eager-loading the relation in the initial query.

Django expresses eager loading as a join for forward foreign keys and as a separate batched query for reverse and many-to-many relations; SQLAlchemy offers joined and select-in loading for the same choice.
Passwords are stored with a salted, deliberately slow algorithm such as bcrypt or Argon2 through the framework's own hashing helpers, never a bare MD5 or SHA digest.
Cursor pagination is preferred to offset pagination on large or actively written collections, because offsets skip or repeat rows as the underlying data shifts.
traps: The session cookie does not contain the session data. Options describing a serialised or signed copy of the session array in the cookie describe a different design, not PHP's default.
An N+1 problem is a loading-strategy defect, not resource exhaustion; enlarging the connection pool, changing isolation level or caching rows all leave the query count proportional to the result set.

HttpOnly and SameSite are not interchangeable: HttpOnly stops JavaScript reading the cookie and so limits XSS-based theft, while SameSite governs whether the browser attaches it to cross-site requests and so bears on CSRF.
An ORM does not make code injection-proof. Generated queries are parameterised, but a raw SQL fragment or a filter built by string concatenation reintroduces the vulnerability.

Authentication versus authorisation in status codes: a caller with no valid identity gets 401, a caller whose identity is known but insufficient gets 403, and answering 403 to an unauthenticated request hides the fact that credentials were never supplied.
mnem: N plus 1 is exactly what it says: one query for the list, one more for every row it returned. If the query count tracks the number of results, it is a lazy relation.

sub: Git version control, Docker, CI/CD, Linux administration, Nginx and deployment
def: This leaf covers the delivery pipeline of a web application: Git as a content-addressed history of commits and branches, Docker images and containers as the packaging and isolation unit, CI/CD as the automated path from commit to production, Linux and Nginx as the runtime environment and reverse proxy, and the deployment and monitoring practices that keep the result observable.
exp:
Git is a content-addressed object store with a directed acyclic graph laid over it. A blob is file content, a tree is a directory listing of blobs and trees, and a commit is a tree plus author, message and parent pointers, all named by the hash of their content, which is why a commit's identity depends on its entire history and why rewriting anything changes every hash downstream. A branch is nothing but a movable pointer to a commit and HEAD is a pointer to the current branch, which makes branching cheap and explains why switching branches is a working-tree operation rather than a server round trip. Work moves through three areas, the working tree, the index or staging area, and the repository, so add and commit are two distinct decisions. Integration is either a merge, which creates a commit with two parents and leaves both histories intact, or a rebase, which replays your commits onto a new base and therefore gives them new hashes. That last fact is the whole rule about published history: rebase, amend, squash and reset all rewrite, so they are safe only on commits nobody else has pulled. To undo a defective commit that is already on a shared main branch, the correct instrument is revert, which computes the inverse change and records it as a new commit, leaving history append-only; reset with hard moves the branch pointer backwards and discards work, which then requires a force push and breaks every other clone. Two smaller distinctions are asked: fetch downloads remote objects and updates remote-tracking refs without touching your branch while pull is fetch followed by a merge or rebase, and adding a path to gitignore has no effect on a file that is already tracked, which must be removed from the index first.

Docker packages an application as an image, which is an ordered stack of read-only filesystem layers plus metadata, and runs it as a container, which is an ordinary host process isolated by kernel namespaces for process ids, networking, mounts, hostname, IPC and users, and constrained by control groups for CPU and memory. There is no guest kernel and no hypervisor, which is the whole reason a container starts in milliseconds and a virtual machine does not. In the Dockerfile, FROM selects the base, RUN executes at build time and produces a layer, COPY brings files in and is preferred to ADD because ADD additionally unpacks archives and fetches URLs, WORKDIR sets the directory, USER should drop from root before the application runs, ENTRYPOINT declares the executable while CMD supplies default arguments that a docker run argument overrides, and EXPOSE is documentation that publishes nothing on its own. Layer caching rewards ordering instructions from least to most frequently changing, so copying the dependency manifest and installing dependencies before copying application source means a code edit does not reinstall the world. Multi-stage builds compile in one stage and copy only the artefact into a slim runtime stage, keeping compilers and build secrets out of the shipped image. The security consequence to hold onto is that every build-time instruction is preserved in an inspectable layer and in the image history, so a secret written with ENV or passed as ARG can be read by anyone who can pull the image, however many later layers appear to remove it; secrets belong in run-time environment variables, mounted files or a secret manager. Container filesystems are ephemeral, so state goes in a volume or an external service. Where Kubernetes is used, the vocabulary is a pod as the smallest schedulable unit, a Deployment managing a ReplicaSet for rollout and scaling, a Service giving a stable virtual address with load balancing across pods, an Ingress routing HTTP by host and path, and ConfigMaps and Secrets supplying configuration. Two pairs are examinable there: requests are what the scheduler uses to place a pod while limits are the ceiling enforced at run time, where exceeding a memory limit kills the container and exceeding a CPU limit merely throttles it; and a liveness probe failing restarts the container while a readiness probe failing only removes it from the Service's endpoints until it recovers.

Continuous integration means every commit on a shared mainline is automatically built and tested, so integration defects surface in minutes rather than at a merge weeks later. Continuous delivery means the pipeline always leaves a release-ready artefact behind a manual promotion; continuous deployment removes the manual step. A conventional pipeline checks out the code, restores a dependency cache, lints, runs unit tests, builds an artefact or container image, runs integration tests against it, scans dependencies and the image for known vulnerabilities, publishes to a registry with an immutable tag, deploys to staging, and promotes that same artefact to production after smoke tests. Building once and promoting the identical artefact through environments is the discipline that makes staging meaningful; rebuilding per environment means production runs something never tested. Rollout strategies trade risk against cost: rolling replaces instances a few at a time, blue-green keeps a second full environment and switches traffic at the load balancer with an instant rollback, and canary sends a small traffic percentage to the new version while watching error rates. Database migrations must be forward and backward compatible across a rollout, which is the expand-then-contract discipline, because during a rolling deploy both versions of the code run against one schema.

Linux administration on a web server reduces to a few areas that are asked concretely. Permissions are three triads of read, write and execute for owner, group and others, expressed numerically as 755 or 644, with the meanings shifting on a directory: read lists the entry names, write creates and removes entries, and execute grants the right to traverse into it and to resolve a name through it. Because path resolution walks each component in turn, the Nginx worker's user needs execute permission on every directory in the chain, on the parent, on its child and on the site directory, to reach the file at the end of the path, and read permission on the file itself; read alone on the directories is not enough and ownership is not required. The special bits are setuid and setgid, and the sticky bit, which on a world-writable directory such as the temporary directory restricts deletion to the owner of each file. Beyond that: manage services and their restart policy with systemd units and read their output with journalctl, inspect listening sockets with ss, disk usage with df and du, and processes with ps and top; use SSH key authentication with password and direct root login disabled; keep a host firewall closed by default; and rotate logs so a chatty application cannot fill the filesystem and take the site down.

Nginx is event-driven rather than thread-per-connection, running a master process that reads configuration and binds ports and a set of workers that handle many thousands of connections each with non-blocking I O. It serves three roles in a typical deployment: static file server, TLS terminator holding the certificate and its automated renewal, and reverse proxy or load balancer in front of an application server such as PHP-FPM, Gunicorn or Uvicorn defined in an upstream block. Virtual hosts are server blocks selected by server_name; location blocks are matched with a defined precedence in which an exact match wins, then a prefix match marked to stop regex evaluation, then regular expressions in file order, then the longest ordinary prefix; try_files is the directive that serves a file if present and otherwise falls back, which is exactly what a single-page application's history routing needs. Configuration should be validated before it is applied, and a reload replaces workers gracefully so existing connections finish rather than being dropped.

Deployment and monitoring close the loop. Configuration comes from the environment rather than from files baked into the artefact, so one image runs in every environment. Observability rests on metrics, logs and traces: metrics answer how much and how often, structured logs answer what happened in this request, and distributed traces answer where the time went across services, with Prometheus scraping metrics and Grafana displaying them being the common pairing. Alert on user-visible symptoms such as error rate and latency rather than on every resource threshold, and expose health endpoints that a load balancer or orchestrator can poll. Availability arithmetic is worth being able to do in the exam: 99.9 percent allows 0.1 percent of the period as downtime, which is about 8 hours 46 minutes in a 365-day year and about 43 minutes in a 30-day month, while 99.99 percent allows roughly 53 minutes a year.

Exam shape: MCQ items on this leaf are operational scenarios with one correct action, on undoing a pushed commit, on why a static file returns 403, on where a secret must not be placed. The conventional half is broad and reliably essay-shaped, typically explain a CI/CD pipeline for a government web application from commit to production, or compare containers with virtual machines and describe container orchestration, and marks come from naming stages and mechanisms in order rather than from listing tool names.
facts: git revert records a new commit that inverts a change and is the safe way to undo a commit already pushed to a shared branch; git reset --hard moves the branch pointer and discards history, requiring a force push.
A Git branch is a movable pointer to a commit, and rebase replays commits onto a new base, giving them new hashes, which is why it must not be used on published history.
git fetch updates remote-tracking references without changing your branch; git pull is a fetch followed by a merge or rebase.
Containers share the host kernel and are isolated by namespaces and control groups, with no guest operating system or hypervisor involved.
ENTRYPOINT declares the executable and CMD supplies default arguments that a docker run argument overrides; EXPOSE only documents a port and publishes nothing.
Anything set at build time with ENV or ARG is preserved in an inspectable image layer and in the image history, so secrets must be supplied at run time instead.
In Kubernetes, requests drive scheduling and limits are enforced at run time; exceeding a memory limit terminates the container while exceeding a CPU limit only throttles it.
A failing liveness probe restarts the container; a failing readiness probe only removes the pod from the Service's endpoints until it passes again.
On a directory the execute bit grants traversal, so a process needs execute permission on every directory along a path plus read permission on the target file to read it.
The sticky bit on a world-writable directory restricts deletion of an entry to its owner, which is why the shared temporary directory is safe to write in.
Nginx location matching resolves an exact match first, then a prefix match marked to skip regular expressions, then regular expressions in configuration order, then the longest ordinary prefix.
An availability target of 99.9 percent permits roughly 8 hours 46 minutes of downtime a year, or about 43 minutes in a 30-day month.
traps: revert versus reset: both undo, but only revert is safe once the commit is published. An option offering reset --hard or an interactive rebase to remove a pushed commit is rewriting shared history.
Read permission on a directory is not enough to open a file inside it. Read lists names, execute traverses, and the traverse right is needed on every parent directory as well as the last one.

Placing a secret in the Dockerfile and deleting it in a later layer does not remove it, because earlier layers remain in the image; the wrong answers here claim run-time variables are encrypted or that build-time variables are invisible to the process.
CMD versus ENTRYPOINT: arguments given to docker run replace CMD but are appended to ENTRYPOINT, so an image that must always run one binary should declare it as ENTRYPOINT.

Liveness versus readiness probes: using a liveness probe for a slow dependency causes restart loops, because liveness failure kills the container while readiness failure only takes it out of rotation.
mnem: On a directory, x means search, not run, and you need it on every link of the path. In Git, revert is public and reset is private.
